name: Hoop skirt

card.summary: A cage of steel or cane hoops worn under a skirt to widen the silhouette into a bell shape, making the waist look smaller and the outfit more dramatic.
card.note: Historically linked to snagging, tipping and fire accidents.

quick.overview:
A hoop skirt is an undergarment made of concentric hoops of steel, cane or whalebone joined by fabric tapes, worn beneath a skirt to hold it out in a wide bell or dome. By widening the lower half of the outfit, it makes the waist look narrower and creates a pronounced hourglass shape.

The cage crinoline was patented in Paris in 1856 and dominated 1850s and 1860s fashion before giving way to the bustle. Hoops have returned repeatedly, from Christian Dior's 1947 New Look to modern wedding, prom and quinceanera gowns and historical costume.
quick.how: The hoop skirt is worn over a chemise and corset and under petticoats and the outer skirt. Modern versions use lightweight steel or plastic boning, and net petticoats (crinolines) give similar volume with less structure. It is used for formal gowns, costume, and styles such as rockabilly or steampunk.
quick.risks: In the 1850s and 1860s the wide hoops snagged on carriages, furniture and machinery, were blown by wind, and increased the danger of skirt fires. Florence Nightingale estimated at least 630 women died from clothing fires in 1863 to 1864. Modern wearers manage doorways, seating and movement.

lead: A hoop skirt, also called a cage crinoline, is a structure of flexible hoops of steel, cane or whalebone that supports a woman's skirt in a wide bell or dome [1][2]. By adding width at the hem, it makes the waist look smaller in comparison, which is how it works for appearance: the silhouette is reshaped by the frame rather than by the body.

Earlier forms include the Spanish verdugado, a conical farthingale of cane hoops from the late 15th century, and the side-extending panniers of the 18th century [1]. The modern cage was patented in France in April 1856 by Angelique Caroline Milliet, and her British agent filed a British patent for a steel skeleton petticoat in July 1856 [2].

The fashion peaked in the late 1850s, when London's Thomson factory produced up to 4,000 hoops a day, and faded after about 1866 as the bustle took over [2]. Revivals in the late 1930s, Dior's 1947 New Look, Vivienne Westwood's 1980s mini-crini and John Galliano and Alexander McQueen's designs have kept the silhouette in fashion [2].

chain: Hoops hold the skirt out from the legs
Wide hem makes the waist look smaller
angle.text: The wide frame creates a bell-shaped skirt that contrasts with a corseted or fitted waist, so the waist reads as narrower. It is worn for formal gowns, weddings, costume and vintage-inspired style.

paras: A hoop skirt consists of graduated rings joined by vertical tapes, with the smallest near the waist and the largest at the hem, and is worn under multiple petticoats [1]. It differs from the earlier crinoline, which meant a stiff horsehair and cotton or linen fabric used in petticoats, and from the bustle, which projects volume toward the back [1][2].

At its widest in the 1860s, the hem of a cage crinoline could measure around 5.5 to 6 yards in circumference by one historian's estimate [2]. Whalebone, cane, gutta-percha and inflatable rubber were tried, but steel became the most popular material [2].

The word crinoline entered use by 1829 for a stiff fabric of horsehair and cotton, and by about 1839 horsehair petticoats were common [2]. In the US, David Hough Jr. patented a caged design in 1846 [1]. After the 1856 Paris patent, large-scale manufacture made hoops affordable, and a New York factory made 3,000 to 4,000 a day in 1859 [2].

From about 1866 skirts shrank, the half-hooped crinolette bridged to the bustle, and the bustle largely replaced the crinoline by the early 1870s [2]. Cage crinolines returned in the 1880s to support large bustles [2]. Edward Molyneux and Norman Hartnell revived hoops in the late 1930s, Dior's 1947 New Look used stiffened underskirts, and nylon net petticoats were common from the 1950s to the early 1970s [2].

The hoop skirt supports voluminous outer skirts without many layers of heavy petticoats, and was valued by Victorian women for the hourglass shape, especially when paired with corsetry [1]. Today crinolines appear in evening gowns, prom, quinceanera and wedding dresses, in square-dance and clogging costume, and in rockabilly and steampunk styles [2].

Contemporary accounts record hoops snagging on carriages, furniture and machinery, and being lifted by wind [2]. Florence Nightingale estimated at least 630 women died of clothing fires in 1863 to 1864, and the 1863 Santiago church fire, which killed thousands, was worsened by flammable crinoline dresses [2].
No studies found. (A 2000 veterinary report used the phrase hoop-skirt for an Elizabethan collar attached to a primate jacket to protect wounds and catheters, which is unrelated to clothing [3].)

timeline.event: Spanish farthingale (verdugado) appears with cane hoops [1].
David Hough Jr. patents a caged hoop design in the US [1].
Milliet patents the cage crinoline in Paris; British patent for a steel skeleton petticoat follows [2].
Factories in London and New York each make thousands of hoops per day [2].
Crinolines begin to fall out of fashion and shrink [2].
Christian Dior's New Look uses stiffened underskirts [2].
